text:
### What Simple and Compound Interest Are
Simple interest is calculated only on your original amount (the principal).

Compound interest is calculated on the principal plus all the interest you’ve already earned, so interest earns interest.

### How Simple and Compound Interest Differ in Practice
A quick example: $1,000 at 5% per year.

| Dimension | Simple Interest | Compound Interest (annual) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Year 1 earnings | $50 (always 5% of the original $1,000) | $50 |
| Year 2 earnings | $50 | 5% of $1,050 = $52.50 |
| Year 3 earnings | $50 | 5% of $1,102.50 = $55.13 |
| Later years earnings | Continues at $50 per year | Continues and so on |
| After 10 years | $1,000 + $500 = $1,500 | $1,000 × 1.05¹⁰ ≈ $1,629 |

### The Formulas for Calculating Simple and Compound Interest
The formulas:

Simple: A = P(1 + rt)

Compound: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), where n is how many times per year interest is compounded

### Why the Gap Between Simple and Compound Interest Grows Over Time
Simple interest grows by the same fixed amount each period, which is a straight line.

Compound interest grows by a fixed percentage of an ever-larger balance, which is an exponential curve.

In the early years the two are nearly identical, because there’s little accumulated interest to earn interest on.

The gap in year 2 is just 5% of the $50 earned in year 1, or $2.50.

But each year the compounding base is larger, so each year’s “interest on interest” is larger, and that extra amount itself starts earning more interest.

The difference between the two isn’t just growing, it’s growing at an accelerating rate.

You can see it in the 10-year numbers above: the gap is $129.

Stretch it to 30 years and simple interest gives $2,500, while compound gives about $4,322, a gap of over $1,800.

### Factors That Widen the Gap Further
Things that widen the gap further:

A higher interest rate

Longer time horizons

More frequent compounding (monthly vs. annually), though this effect is smaller than rate and time

### How Compounding Works in Savings, Investments, and Debt
This is why compounding works in your favor on savings and investments, and against you on debt like credit cards, where unpaid interest gets added to the balance and starts accruing interest itself.

```diagram
Principal -> Simple Interest: Calculated only on original amount
Principal -> Compound Interest: Base for initial interest
Compound Interest -> Accumulated Interest: Earns interest on interest
Accumulated Interest -> Compound Interest: Added to balance
Debt Balance -> Unpaid Interest: Added to balance
Unpaid Interest -> Debt Balance: Accrues interest itself
```

analysis.main_topic: Difference between simple and compound interest and why the gap grows over time
primary_claims: Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal amount, while compound interest is calculated on the principal plus accumulated interest.
Simple interest grows linearly by a fixed amount each period, whereas compound interest grows exponentially based on an ever-larger balance.
Higher interest rates, longer time horizons, and more frequent compounding widen the gap between simple and compound interest.
Compounding applies to both savings and investments (favorably) and debt like credit cards (unfavorably).
existing_examples: $1,000 at 5% per year calculated over 10 years for both simple and compound interest
30-year comparison yielding $2,500 for simple interest and $4,322 for compound interest
missing_intermediate_steps: Step-by-step algebraic derivation of the compound interest formula from year-over-year multiplication
assumed_prior_knowledge: Basic familiarity with mathematical formulas and exponents
possible_confusions: Distinguishing how the variable 'n' affects the compounding periods within the formula versus annual compounding
ambiguous_references: You can see it in the 10-year numbers above

learning_objectives: Define simple interest and calculate its linear growth over time
Define compound interest and explain the concept of 'interest on interest'
Explain why the gap between simple and compound interest grows exponentially over time
Identify the main factors that widen the gap between simple and compound interest
prerequisite_order: Understanding of time periods in years
explanation_sequence: Define principal, simple interest, and compound interest
Compare side-by-side numerical examples for simple and compound interest over a short period
Introduce simple and compound interest formulas
Explain the geometric and exponential mechanics behind why the gap grows over time
Discuss real-world variables like rate, time, and compounding frequency
Apply the concept to savings versus debt
